title: Between the lines
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: INDIRECTION OPENS ALMOST NOTHING, AND THAT IS THE LESSON. Every device in this module is a USE of something the ladder already owns: a plain statement of fact (L3-M6's experiencer frame, L1-M3's na asti), the optative (L3-M4), the agentless passive (L4-M7) and a question (L1-M2). Two words are new in the whole module. What makes a sentence indirect is where it is said, not what is in it.

THE STATEMENT THAT IS A REQUEST. mahyam jalam na asti says only that the speaker has no water, and it is how water is asked for. Nothing in it asks: there is no kṛpayā, no imperative, no question. The fact is stated and the listener does the rest, which is why this is the politest request on the whole course.

THE OPTATIVE AS A SUGGESTION. bhavān idam pustakam paṭhet suggests; L2-M1's imperative would instruct. It is L3-M4's -et cell doing the job L4-M5 named it for — a hedge — aimed at the listener instead of at a claim. The four cells this course writes are gacchet, khādet, paṭhet and L5-M6's vadet, and no other.

THE REGISTER CHIP BELONGS TO THE SENTENCE AND NOT TO THE ROW. L4-M7 chipped its passive sentences formal because an official notice is formal; the VERB is not. So kriyate and dīyate appear here in neutral sentences, and a tap on either still lands on a gloss that is true of the line in front of you. What does not come across with them is the agent: an indirect sentence names nobody, exactly as an official one does not.

saṅketaḥ is a HINT — something meant to be read between the lines. It is not L4-M7's sūcanā, which is a posted notice and says what it means. Keeping the two apart is the whole distinction this module teaches: a notice is public and explicit, a hint is private and deniable.

English is itself a heavily indirect language, so nothing here asks you to think differently — only to do it with different material. What does NOT carry across is the stack of English modals: there is no 'could you possibly'. Its jobs are done by the optative, by a plain statement of fact, or by L2-M1's kṛpayā with an imperative when the request turns out to be direct after all.

THE MARKING AXIS FLIPS FROM THE HUMOUR MODULE AND THE TWO MUST NOT BE CONFUSED. A joke is MARKED here — L5-M2's kevalam parihāsam frame announces it — and irony is NOT. A learner who has just been taught to frame a joke will try to frame the irony too, deliver it flat, and simply be rude.

SARCASM CANNOT BE WRITTEN IN A DISPLAY, EVEN IN PRINCIPLE. It is the same words in a different frame, so it lives in the usage and sound notes, where the delivery can be described. bhavataḥ kāryam uttamam asti is praise on the page; what makes it the other thing is the room, the face and the pause, and none of those is spelling.

AN INDIRECT PROHIBITION IS STILL NOT mā. The negative imperative has been refused since L1-M3 and is refused here, where an indirect prohibition would reach for it hardest. What this course says instead is L4-M7's na kartavyam, or the impersonal atra evam na kriyate, or simply the statement that makes the point and leaves the conclusion to the listener.

WHAT THIS MODULE DOES NOT TEACH, because other rungs own it. The polite request proper is L2-M1's and is fully paid. Banter is L5-M2's. The honest hedge is L4-M5's, and it doubts a CLAIM rather than veiling a request. A formal apology is L5-M4's. And every -si present and the vocative — which an indirect request to a named person would want — are written nowhere on this course.

words.note: L1-M1's 'to me'. In L3-M6's frame the person stands in this shape and the thing they have — or do not have — is the subject.
L1-M3's water, neuter, and the SUBJECT of this line. Nothing in the sentence asks for it; it is simply reported missing.
L1-M2's 'not'. na asti is fixed: the copula may drop when a sentence is positive and never when it is denied.
L1-M3's copula. With a 'to me' in front of it, it is the whole of 'have', and negated it is the whole of a request.

sentences.trap: There is no request in this sentence and there is not meant to be. Adding kṛpayā or an imperative does not make it politer — it makes it a different, blunter act, and the listener hears the change.
sentences.sound: MAH-yam JA-lam NA AS-ti. Said as a request it falls at the end and the na is unstressed; said as a complaint the na is where the weight goes. Same words, and only the tune tells them apart.

variations.cue: I have water.
variations.changed: the negation is lifted and the sentence stops being a request at all

variations.cue: Please give me water.
variations.changed: the same want said directly, with L2-M1's request machinery — shorter to explain and heavier to say

variations.cue: You have no water.
variations.changed: the lack moves to the listener, and the sentence turns from a request into an offer

sentences.usage: The politest way this course can ask for anything: state the fact and stop. It is deniable on both sides — the speaker asked for nothing and the listener refused nothing — which is exactly what makes it usable with a stranger.
sentences.mnemonic: State the lack; let them fill it.

mistake.why: na asti is fixed. The copula may be dropped when a sentence is positive and never when it is denied, so a bare na leaves the sentence with nothing to negate.

words.note: L1-M7's 'here'. It points at a place instead of naming one, so it takes no ending — and here it points at the room you are both in.
Heat, neuter — the noun and the quality in one word. atra uṣṇam asti is 'there is heat here', which is how this language says it is hot.
L1-M3's 'there is'. With a place word in front, it says what is present where — the same frame L1-M7 used for a book on a table.

sentences.trap: The error is not in the grammar; it is in the hearing. Taken as a remark about the weather, this sentence invites agreement and nothing happens. Taken as it is meant, it asks for a window, and the listener who agrees with it has refused without knowing.
sentences.sound: AT-ra USH-nam AS-ti. The ṣ of uṣṇam is the retroflex sibilant, the tongue curled back, and the ṇ after it is retroflex for the same reason. Said as a hint the line is flat and slightly drawn out on uṣṇam.

mistake.why: Nothing is wrong with these words, and that is the point of putting them here: agreeing with the observation is the mistake. The speaker asked for a window and has been told they are right about the temperature.

variations.cue: It is not hot in here.
variations.changed: denied, which is what the listener says when they are refusing the request without naming it

variations.cue: Is it hot in here?
variations.changed: asked instead of stated, which hands the decision to the listener rather than hinting at it

variations.cue: It is hot in the house.
variations.changed: the pointing word gives way to a named place, and the line stops being about the room you are standing in

sentences.usage: The classic hint, and it works in English too — which is why it is the first one taught. The Sanskrit half worth learning is that the observation carries no request marker at all, so the whole weight falls on where and when it is said.
sentences.mnemonic: Say the room, not the want.

sentences.display: bhavān idam pustakam paṭhet, yataḥ idam uttamam asti.
sentences.cue: You might read this book, because it is excellent.
sentences.literal: your-honour this book might-read, because this excellent is

words.note: L1-M2's polite 'you', with a third-person verb as always. The suggestion is aimed at the listener and the grammar never says so.
L1-M1's 'this', the neuter shape. It is used twice here because L3-M2's tat is a CORRELATIVE and there is no relative clause to answer.
L3-M4's optative of paṭhati. It suggests rather than instructs, which is the whole distance between this and L2-M1's imperative.
L1-M9's 'because', at the front of its own clause. A suggestion with a reason behind it is harder to refuse and easier to accept.
L2-M3's praise, neuter here to agree with idam. It is warm rather than measured, which is what a recommendation wants.

sentences.trap: paṭhet is not weaker than an imperative; it is a different act. The imperative tells somebody what to do and expects it done. The optative offers, and leaves refusing costless — which is why it is the shape a suggestion takes between people who are not close.

variations.cue: You might read this book.
variations.changed: the reason falls away and the suggestion stands bare, which is blunter than it looks

variations.cue: You might read this book.
variations.changed: the listener is a woman, and only the address word moves — the verb never agreed with her

variations.cue: Might you read this book?
variations.changed: the suggestion is asked rather than made, which is as tentative as this course gets

sentences.usage: How a book, a road or a dish is recommended to somebody you are not close to. The reason after yataḥ is not decoration: a bare optative can read as a polite way of telling somebody what to do.
sentences.script: भवान् इदम् पुस्तकम् पठेत्, यतः इदम् उत्तमम् अस्ति।

words.note: L5-M3's 'this way', pointing at a manner and never at a thing. It stands in for whatever the listener has just done.
L4-M7's passive of karoti. Nobody is named as doing it and nobody is named as forbidding it, which is the entire courtesy of the line.

sentences.trap: This is a prohibition with no prohibition word in it. mā has been refused since L1-M3 and is not wanted here: the passive with na says that the thing is not among the things done, and the listener draws the rest.

variations.cue: That is how it is done here.
variations.changed: the negation lifts and the same frame becomes an instruction instead of a correction

variations.cue: That is not done there.
variations.changed: the place moves away from the listener, which takes all the edge out of the sentence

variations.cue: That should not be done here.
variations.changed: the passive gives way to L4-M1's gerundive, which states an obligation where the passive stated a custom

sentences.usage: How a stranger is corrected without being accused. The passive takes the person out of it twice over — nobody does it and nobody is told not to — and the same sentence in the active would name somebody and sting.
sentences.mnemonic: Name the custom, not the culprit.

mistake.why: The passive ends -te and not -ti. kriyate belongs to the set L1-M1's rocate belongs to, and the -ti was copied across from the active karoti.

sentences.display: kim bhavān adya sāyam gṛhe asti?
sentences.cue: Are you at home this evening?
sentences.literal: question your-honour today in-the-evening at-home is

words.note: L1-M2's kim at the front, turning the statement into a yes/no question. Here the question is the invitation and there is no other.
L1-M4's 'today'. It never bends and never takes anything in front of it — a time word simply stands in the sentence.
L1-M4's 'in the evening'. The -am is part of the word and not an object ending: nothing is being acted on.
L1-M6's house in the 'in' shape. Asking where somebody will be is how a visit is proposed without proposing one.

sentences.trap: This is not a question about somebody's timetable. Answered with a bare ām it has done nothing; answered with ām plus an invitation it has done its work, and a learner who takes it at face value has missed a visit.

variations.display: kim bhavatī adya sāyam gṛhe asti?
variations.cue: Are you at home this evening?
variations.changed: the listener is a woman, and the address word is the only thing that moves
variations.script: किम् भवती अद्य सायम् गृहे अस्ति?

variations.cue: You are at home this evening.
variations.changed: asserted rather than asked, which turns an invitation into an observation

variations.display: kim bhavān śvaḥ sāyam gṛhe asti?
variations.cue: Are you at home tomorrow evening?
variations.changed: the day moves forward, which is the safer version: tonight is short notice in any language
variations.script: किम् भवान् श्वः सायम् गृहे अस्ति?

sentences.usage: The question that is an invitation. It gives the listener two clean exits — they may be busy, or they may simply answer the question — and neither costs anybody anything.
sentences.script: किम् भवान् अद्य सायम् गृहे अस्ति?

sentences.display: saḥ kevalam saṅketaḥ āsīt, ataḥ aham na kruddhaḥ.
sentences.cue: That was only a hint, so I am not angry.
sentences.literal: that only hint was, so I not angry

words.note: L1-M5's 'he · that one', masculine to agree with saṅketaḥ. A masculine thing takes this word as readily as a man does.
L5-M2's 'only', the word that cuts something down to size. In the joke module it shrank a joke; here it shrinks a hint.
A hint, masculine — something meant to be read between the lines. It is NOT L4-M7's sūcanā, which is a posted notice and says what it means.
L4-M8's one imperfect, third singular. It says how something stood, which is what a hint already given did.
L3-M6's 'angry', an adjective agreeing with the speaker: kruddhaḥ from a man, kruddhā from a woman.

sentences.trap: saṅketaḥ and sūcanā are not interchangeable. A sūcanā is posted, public and explicit; a saṅketaḥ is private and deniable. Calling somebody's hint a sūcanā accuses them of having said it outright.
sentences.sound: SAH KAY-va-lam sang-KAY-tah AA-seet, A-tah a-HAM NA KRUD-dhah. The ṅ of saṅketaḥ is the ng of 'sing', shaped by the k behind it; the dh of kruddhaḥ is one aspirated d and not d plus h.

variations.cue: That was only a hint.
variations.changed: the consequence drops and the line becomes a plain correction of what was heard

variations.display: saḥ kevalam saṅketaḥ āsīt, ataḥ aham na kruddhā.
variations.cue: That was only a hint, so I am not angry.
variations.changed: a woman is speaking, and the adjective at the end is the only word that knows it
variations.script: सः केवलम् सङ्केतः आसीत्, अतः अहम् न क्रुद्धा।

variations.display: saḥ saṅketaḥ na āsīt, ataḥ aham kruddhaḥ.
variations.cue: That was not a hint, so I am angry.
variations.changed: both halves flip together, which is the retraction refused rather than accepted
variations.script: सः सङ्केतः न आसीत्, अतः अहम् क्रुद्धः।

sentences.usage: What you say when an indirect line has been taken badly. Naming the hint as a hint is the repair, and kevalam is what makes it a repair and not a defence.
sentences.script: सः केवलम् सङ्केतः आसीत्, अतः अहम् न क्रुद्धः।

sentences.display: idam na kartavyam iti mama matam.
sentences.cue: My view is that this should not be done.
sentences.literal: this not must-be-done quote of-me opinion

words.note: L4-M1's gerundive of karoti, fixed neuter -am. Negated it is a prohibition that names nobody who must obey it.
L3-M5's quotative, closing the whole judgement so that the sentence can be ABOUT it rather than make it.
L4-M4's opinion in its naming shape. mama matam at the end turns a flat prohibition into one person's position.

sentences.trap: Wrapping the prohibition in mama matam does not weaken it — it moves it. The bare na kartavyam is a rule; with mama matam behind it, it is a view, and a view can be disagreed with, which is what makes it easier to hear.

variations.cue: My view is that this should be done.
variations.changed: the negation lifts and the same frame recommends where it forbade

variations.display: idam na kartavyam iti sūcanā asti.
variations.cue: There is a notice saying this must not be done.
variations.changed: the view becomes a posted notice, which is L4-M7's register and carries no person at all
variations.script: इदम् न कर्तव्यम् इति सूचना अस्ति।

variations.cue: I think this should not be done.
variations.changed: the noun gives way to L3-M3's verb, which is lighter and sounds spoken rather than written

sentences.usage: How a prohibition is offered rather than issued. The gerundive on its own belongs on a wall; behind iti mama matam it belongs in a conversation, and the difference is audible.
sentences.script: इदम् न कर्तव्यम् इति मम मतम्।

sentences.display: adhunā sāyam jātam, ataḥ bhavān gṛham gacchet.
sentences.cue: It is evening now, so you might go home.
sentences.literal: now evening happened, so your-honour home might-go

words.note: L4-M6's 'now'. It marks the moment the observation is made, which is where all of this sentence's force sits.
L2-M8's 'come about', learned whole. sāyam jātam is 'evening has come' — a fact reported, with nobody doing anything.
L1-M6's house as the place gone TO. No word for 'to' is written: the -am is the whole of it.
L3-M4's optative of gacchati. It is the gentlest way this course has of telling somebody the evening is over.

sentences.trap: The fact does the work and the optative only finishes it. Said without adhunā sāyam jātam, bhavān gṛham gacchet is close to an instruction to leave, and the observation in front of it is what makes it hospitable instead.

variations.display: adhunā sāyam jātam, ataḥ bhavān gṛham gacchatu.
variations.cue: It is evening now, so please go home.
variations.changed: the optative gives way to the polite imperative, which asks outright and is a heavier thing to say
variations.script: अधुना सायम् जातम्, अतः भवान् गृहम् गच्छतु।

variations.cue: It is evening now.
variations.changed: the suggestion falls away entirely, leaving the observation to do all of it — which is often enough

variations.display: adhunā sāyam jātam, ataḥ bhavatī gṛham gacchet.
variations.cue: It is evening now, so you might go home.
variations.changed: the guest is a woman, and only the address word moves
variations.script: अधुना सायम् जातम्, अतः भवती गृहम् गच्छेत्।

sentences.usage: How a visit is ended without ending it. Note the order: the fact first, the suggestion second. Reversed, the suggestion arrives before its reason and the guest hears only the door.
sentences.mnemonic: The clock says it; you only agree.
sentences.script: अधुना सायम् जातम्, अतः भवान् गृहम् गच्छेत्।

mistake.display: adhunā sāyaḥ jātam, ataḥ bhavān gṛham gacchet.
mistake.why: sāyam is 'in the evening' and its -am is part of the word, not an ending that can be swapped. There is no sāyaḥ: L1-M4 taught the word whole and it has one shape.

sentences.display: atra bhojanam na dīyate, kintu jalam dīyate.
sentences.cue: Food is not served here, but water is.
sentences.literal: here meal not is-given, but water is-given

words.note: L2-M5's meal, neuter, and the subject of a passive verb: the thing given is what a passive sentence is about.
L4-M7's passive of dadātu. Here it does a conversational job rather than an official one, and the row's gloss holds for both.
L1-M10's 'but', opening its clause. It is what turns a refusal into an offer of something else.

sentences.trap: Nobody refuses anything in this sentence. The passive keeps the person who would have said no out of it, and the kintu half means the listener is not left with nothing — which is the difference between a refusal and a rebuff.

variations.cue: Food is not served here.
variations.changed: the offer is withdrawn and the line becomes a flat refusal

variations.display: atra bhojanam dīyate, kintu jalam na dīyate.
variations.cue: Food is served here, but water is not.
variations.changed: the two halves swap, which is the same courtesy pointed the other way
variations.script: अत्र भोजनम् दीयते, किन्तु जलम् न दीयते।

variations.cue: Is food served here?
variations.changed: asked rather than announced, which is the guest's side of the same exchange

sentences.usage: The shape of a refusal that does not sting: say what is not available in the passive, then say what is. The second half is not politeness for its own sake — without it the passive sounds like a rule rather than a fact.
sentences.script: अत्र भोजनम् न दीयते, किन्तु जलम् दीयते।

sentences.display: bhavataḥ kāryam uttamam asti iti aham vadāmi.
sentences.cue: I say your work is excellent.
sentences.literal: of-your-honour work excellent is quote I say

words.note: L1-M2's polite 'you' in its 'of' shape. It owns the work, and it is the only word in the line that points at the listener.

words.cue: work · the thing to be done
words.note: L3-M2's work as a thing done rather than a place gone to. Neuter, so the adjective on it ends -am.
L2-M7's verb of saying, first person. Saying that you are saying it is what makes praise sound weighed rather than automatic.

sentences.trap: On the page this is praise and nothing else. What turns the same words into their opposite is delivery — a flat tone, a pause before uttamam, a face that disagrees — and none of that is spelling. This is why sarcasm is described in these notes and written in no line of this course.
sentences.sound: bha-va-TAH KAAR-yam ut-ta-MAM AS-ti I-ti a-HAM va-DAA-mi. Meant straight, the weight lands on uttamam and the line rises. Meant the other way, uttamam is flattened and stretched and everything after it falls away.

variations.cue: Your work is excellent.
variations.changed: the frame drops and the praise stands bare, which is warmer and less considered

variations.display: bhavatyāḥ kāryam uttamam asti iti aham vadāmi.
variations.cue: I say your work is excellent.
variations.changed: the person praised is a woman, and only her word moves
variations.script: भवत्याः कार्यम् उत्तमम् अस्ति इति अहम् वदामि।

variations.display: bhavataḥ kāryam uttamam na asti iti aham na vadāmi.
variations.cue: I do not say your work is not excellent.
variations.changed: both halves negated, which is a real and uncomfortable move: it withholds the praise while refusing to withdraw it
variations.script: भवतः कार्यम् उत्तमम् न अस्ति इति अहम् न वदामि।

sentences.usage: Praise, written plainly, and the module's last point: irony is not a form of words here, so it cannot be learned from a page. Deliver it wrong in a second language and you have not been ironic — you have been rude, and nobody will tell you.
sentences.mnemonic: Irony is delivery, and delivery is not spelling.
sentences.script: भवतः कार्यम् उत्तमम् अस्ति इति अहम् वदामि।

comprehensionPool.display: mahyam jalam na asti, kṛpayā jalam dadātu.
comprehensionPool.cue: I have no water — please give me some.
comprehensionPool.script: मह्यम् जलम् न अस्ति, कृपया जलम् ददातु।

comprehensionPool.display: atra uṣṇam asti, ataḥ aham gṛham gacchāmi.
comprehensionPool.cue: It is hot in here, so I am going home.
comprehensionPool.script: अत्र उष्णम् अस्ति, अतः अहम् गृहम् गच्छामि।

comprehensionPool.display: atra evam na kriyate iti niyamaḥ asti.
comprehensionPool.cue: There is a rule that this is not done here.
comprehensionPool.script: अत्र एवम् न क्रियते इति नियमः अस्ति।

comprehensionPool.display: kim bhavān śvaḥ sāyam kāryālaye asti?
comprehensionPool.cue: Are you at the office tomorrow evening?
comprehensionPool.script: किम् भवान् श्वः सायम् कार्यालये अस्ति?

comprehensionPool.cue: A notice saying this must not be done.
I have no time just now.

comprehensionPool.display: atra jalam dīyate, kintu bhojanam na dīyate.
comprehensionPool.cue: Water is served here, but food is not.
comprehensionPool.script: अत्र जलम् दीयते, किन्तु भोजनम् न दीयते।

comprehensionPool.cue: My hint was only a joke.
